description: Cordage is made by twisting plant or animal fibres into strands, then plying strands in the opposite direction. The oldest direct find is a tiny three-ply cord, probably of inner-bark fibre, on a Neanderthal stone tool at Abri du Maras, France, roughly 41,000 to 52,000 years old. Lashing, nets, snares and carrying depend on it.
uncertainty: Older cordage is inferred (hafting, beads, possible string-wear) but not directly preserved; the Abri du Maras date is a range and the fibre identification is probable, not certain.

description: Basketry interlaces stiff plant materials by twining, coiling or plaiting into containers, mats, sieves and fish traps. Fibres rarely survive, so early evidence is often indirect: twined impressions on fired clay at Pavlov and Dolní Věstonice, Czech Republic, about 27,000 years old. Dry Guitarrero Cave in Peru preserved twined plant artefacts roughly 12,000 to 10,000 years old.
uncertainty: Basketry is almost certainly older than its surviving evidence; whether the Pavlov and Dolni Vestonice impressions are basketry or textile is debated, and the Guitarrero Cave dates have been revised (direct dating places some items near 12,000 years ago).

description: A framed hut uses posts, poles or large bones as a skeleton, covered with hides, brush or turf, giving shelter that can be reoccupied across seasons. Hut traces at Dolní Věstonice in Moravia date to about 26,000 years ago; on the Ukrainian plain, the Mezhyrich dwellings of interlocked mammoth bones are later, about 18,000 years old.
uncertainty: Mezhyrich was long dated between about 19,000 and 12,000 years ago; a 2025 radiocarbon study places one structure at about 18,000 years ago, and reading the structures as dwellings remains an interpretation. The proposal's emerged field pairs Mezhirich with about 25 kya, which these dates do not support. Much older shelters have been claimed (e.g., Terra Amata) but are disputed.

description: Wool is the fine, crimped underfleece of domestic sheep. uncertainty: When woolly fleece arose and spread is debated (estimates range across the fifth to third millennia BCE); evidence is indirect (kill-off patterns, texts, spindle whorls, rare textiles).

description: Mudbrick is earth mixed with water and often straw or dung, shaped by hand or in moulds and dried in the sun. Hand-shaped bricks were used at Jericho by roughly 9,000 BCE, and Çatalhöyük in Anatolia was a dense mudbrick town by about 7,000 BCE. uncertainty: Earliest mudbrick dates depend on the dating of Pre-Pottery Neolithic levels at Jericho and other Levantine sites; mould-made bricks are later than hand-shaped ones.

description: The warp-weighted loom hangs vertical warp threads from a beam, kept taut by bunches of clay or stone weights; the weaver stands and beats each weft upward. uncertainty: The proposal dates it to ~5,000 BCE; how early Egyptian basins were artificial, and how far they were centrally organised, is debated. Similar flood farming developed on the Indus and elsewhere.

description: Water-lifting wheels raise water above a river or canal to fields beyond gravity's reach. The saqiya, an animal-driven geared wheel carrying a chain of pots, is attested in Ptolemaic Egypt by about the third century BCE. uncertainty: Dating of the saqiya and the current-driven noria is debated (third to first centuries BCE); the proposal dates the stream-driven wheel to ~100 CE.

description: Gear trains pass rotation between toothed wheels, changing speed, force or direction. The Antikythera mechanism, a bronze device recovered from a shipwreck off a Greek island, used dozens of small gears to calculate positions of the sun and moon and to predict eclipses; it was built around the second or first century BCE. Right-angled gears drove Roman watermills.
uncertainty: The mechanism's construction date is debated (estimates from about 200 to 60 BCE); geared devices were also made in Han China.

description: A pattern loom stores a woven design in its harness: warp threads are tied to cords grouped so each pattern row can be lifted in turn. Han-dynasty loom models from Laoguanshan, of the later second century BCE, are China's earliest evidence of pattern looms. Drawlooms later wove figured silks in Persia, Byzantium and Italy, until French inventors automated them.
uncertainty: Whether the Laoguanshan models are drawlooms or multi-heddle pattern looms is debated (specialists describe a multiple-heddle pattern device); the developed drawloom is usually dated to Tang China (by about 700 CE).

description: Type founding casts many identical metal letters. Each letter is cut in relief on a hard punch, struck into a softer copper matrix, and the matrix fitted into an adjustable hand mould for pouring molten alloy. Johannes Gutenberg developed this system in Strasbourg and Mainz around the 1440s. Earlier movable type in China and Korea was made by other methods.
uncertainty: Gutenberg's exact methods and alloy are reconstructed from later practice and analysis of early type; the role of punches versus sand casting in his earliest type is debated.

description: A navigation canal is a built waterway for freight boats, often crossing a watershed with locks and with reservoirs that feed water to its summit level. China's Grand Canal had crossed summits centuries earlier.
uncertainty: China's Lingqu canal (3rd century BCE) and the Grand Canal's Huitong section (1289; water supply rebuilt 1411) are earlier summit canals; the Canal du Midi was in use by 1681 but final works continued to 1694; the proposal's anchor records the European dates.

uncertainty: Slide rests and screw-cutting lathes existed earlier (e.g., in 16th-18th-century European workshops); Maudslay's role was combination and precision rather than first invention.
